transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-04-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Laura (Peregrine Head of ML), Marcus (Platform Eng), Priya (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy): Deep dive on KV cache eviction and paging during long sessions; discussed batching and quantization tradeoffs; next steps are to run a Dedicated trial and share docs.

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving out time. quick roll call?
00:08 Laura: Hi Maya, Laura here.
00:10 Marcus: Marcus on from infra.
00:12 Priya: Priya, security.
00:14 Ethan: Ethan from Redwood SE.
:16 Maya: ok great, quick agenda — we want to walk through kv cache internals, reproduce Peregrine's eviction pattern, and put together a benchmark plan.
01:02 Ethan: I can share my screen, i'll start with high-level cache architecture, then we'll dig into eviction heuristics and paging. bear with me, the slide auto-layout is a bit off.
01:35 Ethan: so, at a high level our runtime keeps a KV cache per model shard, right, it's a combination of GPU-resident KV + meta-index in host memory. when sequence lengths get long or a lot of concurrent prefixes hit, we have eviction windows that free GPU slots and either flush to host or let the KV be recomputed.
02:10 Laura: quick q — when you say "flush to host" do you mean paging to host DRAM or is there a temp SSD spill?
02:18 Ethan: mostly host DRAM, we don't page to disk in production by default, disk spill is an option but we don't recommend for low-latency SLOs. sometimes the transcriber shows "V-B-C" instead of VPC — sorry about that.
02:45 Marcus: Our traffic patterns are weird — mix of short chat sessions and occasional very long analyst sessions, those long ones seem to trigger evictions and we see latency spikes.
03:05 Ethan: yep that's classic. eviction is triggered by per-shard capacity *and* by a configured soft limit we call the working set threshold. when the active KV exceeds that threshold we evict LRU-ish entries, but the heuristics try to be prefix-aware — pref rank + recency — but it's probabilistic under heavy load, you'll get collisions.
03:42 Priya: collision meaning prefix reuse across different customers? can that leak sensitive context?
03:50 Ethan: great question — no cross-tenant leaks. prefix reuse is an internal dedupe within a tenant's cache indexing layer; we keep tenant namespaces separate. but there are still prefix collisions within a tenant if two sessions share similar tokens and it's deduped to save memory — that can change generation behavior slightly.
04:20 Laura: we saw some strange token drift mid-session, like earlier context seemed to get forgotten and model re-asked for clarification. could that be eviction?
04:33 Ethan: yes, if the KV for earlier tokens got evicted then the model only has the compressed prompt state and will re-query or hallucinate. also note batching can alter when cache entries are materialized — large batches may cause transient cache pressure.
05:05 Ethan: quick note on quantization: 4-bit and 8-bit quant reduce KV footprint, but we observed in our internal tests that certain kernels are less numerically stable, sometimes causing slightly different logits. for long-context stability we often recommend mixed precision: 8-bit KV with calibration.
05:40 Marcus: that resonates; our infra uses 4-bit to save RAM, but we may have to bump to 8 for long state sessions. what's the perf hit?
05:48 Ethan: typically 5-15% token throughput regression depending on kernel and hardware. but it reduces eviction frequency because KV size shrinks, so net latency for long sessions can improve.
06:20 Laura: you mentioned paging — is there a recommended threshold where paging starts and we should avoid long-live sessions?
06:27 Ethan: recommended is to keep working set <75% of GPU KV capacity for steady SLOs. once you push beyond 90% you'll get aggressive evictions and paging. we'll provide tooling to profile your observed working set distribution.
07:05 Marcus: can we pin certain session prefixes to GPU so the analyst workflows never lose KV?
07:13 Ethan: yes — we have a pinning API for hot prefixes, you can mark session IDs as pinned and they won't be evicted until memory pressure forces a global GC. pinning increases memory cost but is useful for SLA'd flows.
07:45 Priya: from security side, for private deployments — if we run in our VPC/on-prem and use KMS, does Redwood's runtime access our keys? how does encryption interact with eviction/paging?
08:02 Ethan: great — in Private mode, the runtime can be configured to use your KMS/HSM for model weights and ephemeral keys for traffic. KV paging to host DRAM is still unencrypted by default because it's in-host memory, but we support mlock and kernel-level protections and process isolation. we can also enable encrypted swap on disk if you opt into disk spill (but again that impacts latency).
08:50 Priya: ok we'll need that documented for our auditors — SOC2 scope, KMS integration flow, and proof that no unencrypted dumps go to shared disk.
09:12 Maya: noted, we'll include our Private deployment security whitepaper and the KMS integration steps.
09:30 Ethan: back to eviction — another subtle thing is prefix reuse across sessions. if two sessions share the same first N tokens, the cache may reuse the same KV entries and you can get token-level coupling. This is intentional for efficiency but can surprise deterministic tests.
10:10 Laura: any strategies to avoid that coupling?
10:15 Ethan: yes — namespace isolation (per-session namespace) removes reuse but increases memory. or use hashed per-session salt when indexing. we usually recommend hybrid: reuse for ephemeral sessions, isolate for regulated workflows.
11:00 Marcus: our logs show sudden spikes in host-to-gpu copies at minute marks that coincide with cron-like batch jobs. could batching/burst traffic be evicting and causing re-materialization?
11:18 Ethan: absolutely. batching bursts create transient high concurrency which increases instantaneous working set. our runtime has a burst-aware throttle and can spill less aggressively if you enable burst buckets. but config tuning is needed — default is conservative.
12:00 Ethan: also, if your batching latency budgets allow, increasing max batch size can reduce overall cache pressure because more tokens are serviced with fewer kernel invocations, but it depends on your latency SLO.
12:40 Laura: about observability — we want token-level tracing and per-route cache hit/miss rates. what do you export?
12:50 Ethan: we have token-level metrics: per-shard KV size, hit-rate, eviction-rate, host spill counts, and histograms for re-materialization latency. we can push to Prometheus and provide dashboards in Redwood Console; we'll share a sample dashboard JSON.
13:30 Marcus: any known bugs where eviction algorithm thrashes because of worst-case workloads?
13:38 Ethan: we had a prior issue (fixed Q4 2026) where certain repeating-prefix workloads caused oscillation due to a TTL miscalculation — that is fixed in runtime v2.3.2. if you're on older runtime you could see thrashing.
14:05 Priya: runtime upgrades in Private mode — what's the procedure?
14:12 Maya: for Private we do staged upgrades, canary on a subset of nodes, and provide release notes. We'll coordinate with your ops team.
14:40 Ethan: demo time — i want to reproduce Peregrine's pattern. Marcus, can you describe a concrete user trace?
14:50 Marcus: sure — analyst sessions start with a 20k-token doc ingest then interactive Q/A over 45–60 minutes; concurrent analysts ~8 per node. we see evictions around 30–40 minutes.
15:20 Ethan: ok i can approximate that locally; i'll run a long-context session with heavy prefix overlap and 8 concurrent sessions to watch working set growth.
16:00 Ethan: while that runs, quick note on quantization + kernel selection: certain GPU kernels prefer 8-bit KV layout; on some hardware (A100 vs H100) the performance tradeoffs shift, so kernel selection matters. we'll include kernel hints for your hardware.
16:40 Laura: our deployment is on-prem with H100s, and we also have some CPU fallback nodes for cold starts. any gotchas?
16:52 Ethan: H100s are great for throughput; if you use CPU fallback for cold starts, watch the serialization format — moving KV from CPU to GPU needs format conversion which adds latency. keep a warm pool of small GPU nodes to avoid conversions.
17:30 Marcus: about prefix reuse — is there a way to run a diagnostic to see which prefixes are being shared most?
17:40 Ethan: yes, we have an index profiler that outputs top-N prefixes by frequency and their memory share. we'll run that against your anonymized logs.
18:10 Priya: we need to ensure the profiler output doesn't include PII; can you run it on hashed tokens or only structural telemetry?
18:20 Ethan: absolutely — we can hash tokens client-side or produce only frequency/bucket counts without token contents.
18:40 Laura: one more — when evicted KV is recomputed, do you recompute from raw tokens or from a checkpointed intermediate?
18:52 Ethan: recompute from raw tokens using the tokenizer and model state. we don't store intermediate checkpoints for every session due to cost; instead we rely on efficient recompute kernels and re-use of cached layers when possible.
19:30 Marcus: what's the regression risk if we flip to pinning hot sessions? Are there edge cases?
19:38 Ethan: pinning reduces eviction but increases OOM risk; if multiple hot sessions pin you'll need larger GPU or more nodes. we suggest pins for small percentage of flows (top 5%).
20:10 Maya: jumping ahead to benchmarking — we'll run two experiments: one simulating your analyst long-session pattern and one synthetic worst-case repeating-prefix to test thrash. we'll capture per-token latency, eviction counts, host spill counts, and kernel timings.
21:00 Marcus: sounds good. what perf delta should we expect if we move from 4-bit to 8-bit?
21:07 Ethan: expect 5-15% throughput drop but about 30-50% fewer evictions for long-context in our internal tests, net effect usually positive for latency SLOs on long sessions.
21:40 Priya: security question — if we enable disk spill with encrypted swap, does Redwood need key access?
21:50 Ethan: in Private mode you control the encryption keys; if you use your KMS we'll use envelope encryption and the runtime will request ephemeral keys. Redwood control plane does not retain your keys. we'll include diagrams.
22:20 Laura: any guidance on batching config defaults for mixed short+long workloads?
22:26 Ethan: use adaptive batching: keep small latency-first batches for interactive sessions and a burst pool for background jobs. set working set thresholds slightly lower than pure long-context to avoid thrash. we'll send recommended config snippets.
23:10 Marcus: during your internal test, did you ever see prefix reuse change generation semantics enough to fail deterministic tests?
23:22 Ethan: in a few cases, yes — deterministic QA tests that rely on exact token sequences can diverge if reuse happens. fixes: isolated namespace or session salts.
24:00 Laura: ok let's recap real quick — main risks: eviction causing token drift, disk spill latency, prefix reuse coupling, quantization numerical variance, and burst-induced thrash.
24:20 Maya: agreed. next steps? refer to action items.
24:30 Ethan: I'll kick off the Dedicated trial run and share the perf traces; i'll also attach kernel selection notes.
24:45 Priya: We'll validate SOC2 scope and get back on any audit requirements.
25:00 Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with docs and schedule the benchmark review.
